title: Sony Music, Warner sue Anthropic, alleging a “brazen campaign” of intellectual property theft
abstract: Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell and numerous other music publishers have sued Anthropic and co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann, alleging the AI lab conducted a “brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works.” The lawsuit, which was filed late Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, was first reported by Music Business Worldwide . The publishers accuse Anthropic of “blatant theft” by using thousands of copyrighted works to train its AI model Claude. “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court,” an Anthropic spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch. This isn’t the first intellectual property lawsuit Anthropic has faced. Some of the same lawyers behind this lawsuit also represent Concord Music Group and Universal Music Group in a case filed in January and led the Bartz v. Anthropic case, in which a group of authors accused Anthropic of using copyrighted works to train products like Claude. Anthropic was ordered to pay $1.5 billion in the landmark Bartz case after a judge ruled that while it was legal for the AI lab to use copyrighted works, it was not legal to acquire that content through piracy. While the cases make similar arguments, there are key differences. This latest lawsuit is particularly broad and builds off the other cases, including by accusing Anthropic of “flagrant piracy” through illegal torrenting to obtain millions of copies of books, including those that contain lyrics and sheet music. Article was updated to include Anthropic’s comment.

title: “We’re not doing 30 bets a year”: Vijay Pande on betting small after running $4 billion at a16z
abstract: It used to be that Vijay Pande was better known in academic circles than investor circles. That changed pretty abruptly a dozen years ago, when Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz — who’d spent their firm’s first five years explicitly avoiding healthcare and life sciences — decided the category was worth betting on after all and handed the keys to Pande. At the time, he was a Stanford chemistry professor who was best known for building Folding@home, the distributed-computing project that turned millions of home PCs into a supercomputer for disease research. Over the next decade-plus, he grew a16z’s bet into a practice managing close to $4 billion. So it was somewhat unexpected when in June of last year, Pande walked away from it all to start something much smaller. In fact, his new firm, VZVC , co-founded with longtime investor Zach Werner, is built around a handful of concentrated bets a year rather than dozens, it has no associates, and it relies heavily on AI for its day-to-day operations. To learn more about Pande’s hard pivot, we talked with him this week about why he’s making just a handful of concentrated bets rather than spreading himself thin in the current market — and about one of the more interesting conundrums in AI-driven biotech: unlike text, biological data can’t be scraped off the internet, so nearly every company ends up building its own walled-off dataset. What does that mean for all the advances AI in medicine has promised, and who actually gets access to them? This conversation has been edited for length and clarity. You can also listen to the fuller conversation (below). You’ve said biology is moving from a “science of discovery” to something you can engineer. What does that mean? For a lot of the way drugs have been developed, there was very much a fortuitous aspect to it. I think what’s shifted is that AI and machine learning allow computers to wrap their type of understanding around something very, very complicated… to try to figure out what targets you want your drugs to hit, for specific diseases, to be able to make those drugs, and now even to help in the clinical trials — which are the most expensive part of the process. I thought clinical trials were getting cheaper because drug developers are using more synthetic data, so not as many people are needed for these trials. That’s, I think, very much an aspiration. The cost and time to get to clinical trials has been shrinking, especially with AI, but it could still cost hundreds of millions of dollars to run a trial, which is why drugs are very expensive. The probability of a drug going successfully from the first trial to the end of the third trial is just 20%. If 8 out of 10 fail, and these things cost hundreds of millions of dollars, the amortized cost gets really high. The reason they fail typically is not that the biologist did something wrong; it’s that all the experiments these drugs were designed on were on animal models like mice, and in the end, animal models are just not very predictive of humans. The AI model is not going to be perfect, but it’s going to be way better than any animal model would be, and once it crosses that bar, that’s where it gets really exciting. [The phase after that is]: Is the drug the right drug for me ? You mean personalized medicine. . . The jargon here is so-called precision medicine. If you go to a doctor with something not trivial, they have to guess what’s going on, because there’s only so much they can tell. Then they give you a drug — and if that doesn’t work, they give you another drug, then another drug. This happens in cancer, it happens in lots of different areas. We would all be much better off if the first drug was the right one. Typically, your blood test values are compared to population averages. But really, they should be compared to: is this [result] weird for you? What we’re starting to do also on the medicine side is [the ability] to just understand what would be right for the individual. Would you say the path to this moment has been slow and steady, or did it spike more recently? I think it’s lots of different things [coming together]. So for instance, precision medicine for the longest time was based on genomics. But the reality is your genome is kind of like the blueprint for your house on day one, but your house is fairly different now compared with the moment it was built. So there are many other things that people can now measure in proteomics and so on that are much more relevant for understanding disease and where your body is now. There has also been [a lot of] automation in robotic measurements that is naturally tied into AI, and those two go hand in hand really well. Over the last decade, there’s been this steady clip fforin both AI for biology and AI for chemistry. The biology part is like, how can we treat this disease? And then the chemistry part is, how can we come up with a drug to go after that specific protein? There have actually been very significant advances over those 10 years. You mentioned that biology is one of the few places AI can’t just scrape data off the internet. What does that mean for how the field develops? It’s a place where you don’t have any of this data that people can just all train the same thing, and your data can’t be distilled from one model to another. It’s a really interesting play from just the pure AI sense. Doesn’t that echo a familiar problem in medicine, though — doctors operating in [territorial, often competitive] silos? You’re onto something really big here. Let’s say [someone] has some type of cancer, and it’s both an issue in oncology and endocrinology — those two doctors really don’t sync together very well. What is really intriguing about AI is that it can, in principle, be a specialist in everything, and it can start to see things that really any single human being couldn’t. It would be equivalent to having a team of the very best doctors all clamoring together in that moment. But is there enough data sharing for that vision to actually be realized? I understand why founders and investors want to protect their [respective findings], but . . . I think one of the bigger trends is that we’re starting to see a shift toward building these atlases of biological information — which, from a technology standpoint, are typically foundation models. And as they become more common, I think we’ll see the same thing that’s happened with open-source LLMs, which do very well against the corporate ones: open-source foundation models in biology having a very broad impact. You’re involved with Genesis Therapeutics, which came out of your lab at Stanford, and Insitro, the drug-discovery company launched by Daphne Koller, a former colleague at Stanford. You say you’re also incubating a company with a founder you’ve known for 20 years. What are you looking for in founders, and in what areas? There are two areas that I’ve been spending most of my time on. One is AI for healthcare delivery, which I did a ton at a16z as well, and then AI for clinical trials. One of the things that’s most important to me [about founders] is that we can really trust each other — founders that have high integrity, that do what they say they’re gonna do… I’m expecting this relationship to be 5, 10 years plus into, ideally, their next company. I want to work with people who are thinking long term like that. Ideally, these are people who are not just trying to win and beat other people, but really thinking about the question: how do we win together? What have you gotten right and wrong in your investing career so far? When I started talking about AI and machine learning and technology and medicine and bio 10 plus years ago, there was a lot of resistance and a lot of people saying, ‘Oh, that’s never going to happen. That’s never going to be useful,’ and so on. That resistance is largely gone and seeing this arc is very fulfilling.

title: Nvidia’s AI advantage is moving beyond the GPU
abstract: Before this week, the dominant story about Nvidia went something like this: For the first few years of the AI boom, Nvidia was the only source for state-of-the-art GPUs, which became immensely profitable as the industry scaled out. In the last few years, hyperscalers like Amazon and Google have started building their own chips, and Nvidia is no longer the only game in town, leading many investors to wonder how durable its advantage really is. It’s a compelling story, and mostly true. After growing its market cap 10x between the start of 2023 and mid-2025, Nvidia shares have been on a more modest trajectory for the past year, driven by concerns about GPU competition. A new narrative has taken shape since the company’s earnings on Wednesday and investors are starting to realize that Nvidia’s advantage goes far beyond GPUs. As AI’s compute grows into the gigawatt scale, orchestration has become an increasingly complex task. Not surprisingly, Nvidia has built much of the state-of-the-art hardware needed to handle it, giving the company a huge advantage in the systems that surround the GPU even as it sees increased competition on the GPUs themselves. For all the talk of compute as a commodity , it’s still incredibly difficult to operate a megascale data center at peak efficiency — and as deployments get bigger and faster, that challenge is only growing. Rack by Rack You can see some of this just by looking at the details of what Nvidia is actually selling. The company is currently rolling out its Vera Rubin architecture, which pairs the Rubin GPU with a collection of other units, including the Vera CPU, the Groq 3 LPX inference accelerator and similar racks for storage and networking. Over the past week, I’ve been talking to folks at Nvidia about what those systems actually do, and the results have been surprising. Like the Rubin GPU itself, they’re extremely specialized systems, but instead of churning through tokens, they’re making sure everything outside the GPU works as efficiently as possible. If the GPU is the engine, these are the rest of the car. The Vera CPU in particular is focused on the problem of orchestrating data. “Vera is important because there’s only so much memory that you can put in a single server or any sort of compute platform,” Jason Hardy, Nvidia’s VP of storage technology, told me. As data centers have scaled up computing power, memory capacity has scaled up too, which is why companies like Micron have gotten rich in the second wave of the infrastructure boom. But getting that data to the GPU at the right time isn’t straightforward — and as companies look to drive tokens-per-watt lower and lower, they’re realizing how important that kind of traffic direction is. “We saw upwards of 3x improvement in these operations, where the Vera CPU is allowing for acceleration,” Hardy said. “So now we can use our flash to its fullest potential, because we can get all that performance out of it without bottlenecking.” You can see versions of the same problem outside of Nvidia. When OpenAI developed its Jalapeño chip, a major focus was avoiding these challenges entirely by minimizing the amount of data that needs to be moved around. “We designed Jalapeño to minimize data movement and communication delays,” the company said in a blog post earlier this month . “Its large domain allows the entire workload to remain within one connected system, minimizing data movement and helping the complete request stay fast and efficient from beginning to end.” It’s a different approach, avoiding data movement entirely by conducting a workload within one integrated chip. But the overall logic is the same, increasing efficiency with smarter traffic control instead of just more processor cycles. That in turn opens up a whole new layer of infrastructure for companies to compete over. This new focus on data orchestration isn’t automatically a win for Nvidia. The company will have to compete with rival chipmakers and hyperscalers just as it has with GPUs. But the competition has moved to a new layer, where building a rival GPU matters less than being able to make the entire system work efficiently. And at least in the early stages, Nvidia looks to have a commanding lead.

title: Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic
abstract: AI Entertainment News Sony Music and Warner Chappell are suing Anthropic The companies call it “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.” The companies call it “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history.” by Terrence O'Brien Aug 29, 2026, 6:19 PM UTC Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. Sony Music and Warner Chappell have filed suit against Anthropic in the US District Court for the Northern District of California seeking damages for “tens of thousands” copyrighted works. The companies are asking for up to $150,000 per work, plus up to $25,000 for each instance when identifiable copyright data was stripped. In total, the damages could amount to several billion dollars if a court finds in Sony and Warner’s favor and awards the maximum amount. This is just the latest high-profile suit against Anthropic, which recently settled a suit brought by the publishing industry for $1.5 billion . It’s also faced multiple lawsuits from Universal Music Group, Concord, and ABKCO, plus separate suits from BMG and Round Hill Music . In addition to suing Anthropic as an entity, the complaint names Co-Founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann as individual defendants. The suit alleges that Mann used BitTorrent to download over five million pirated books , and that employees downloaded at least two million more from Pirate Library Mirror . It also claims that Anthropic scraped lyrics from sites like MusixMatch and LyricFind, which paid to license content from the labels. According to the filing : Plaintiff Music Publishers, a group of the world’s leading music publishers, bring this action to hold accountable the culprits behind one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history. Defendants Anthropic and its founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann have conducted a brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works on a massive scale in order to develop, operate, and reap enormous profits from Anthropic’s “Claude” series of artificial intelligence (“AI”) models. Specific songs named as being found in Anthropic’s training data include Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell’s “Ain’t No Mountain High Enough,” Bon Jovi’s “Livin’ On a Prayer,” Earth, Wind & Fire’s “September,” Leonard Cohen’s “Hallelujah,” and TaylorSwift’s “Paper Rings.” Antrhopic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. title: Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters
abstract: Entertainment AI Tech Musicians-turned-detectives are hunting for AI grifters As AI infiltrates the electronic dance music scene, a callout culture is brewing.﻿ by Charles Pulliam-Moore Aug 29, 2026, 12:00 PM UTC Cath Virginia / The Verge, Max Harris, Getty Images Charles Pulliam-Moore is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years. As audio-focused generative tools and platforms have gotten more sophisticated , the internet has become increasingly filled with AI-generated music whose melodies and vocals are algorithmically derived from the work of human artists. While some of the people pumping out this kind of content immediately own up to using AI , others have denied using the technology until increasing public scrutiny forced them to tell the truth . For musicians — especially those creating art in technologically-focused spaces like electronic dance music — the increasingly complicated question of what is “real” and what isn’t feels particularly urgent and personal. Professional courtesy can make this only more complex; listeners can call out performers they suspect of using gen AI, but it’s something else for artists to raise concerns about their professional peers. There are some though, like 26-year-old EDM producer Max “H4RRIS” Harris, who are taking a stand against generative technology with videos calling out anyone they believe is trying to pass off AI slop as human-made art. When I recently spoke with Harris, he told me that he sees AI-generated music as “a kind of decoy art form,” and he thinks that the people making it don’t really have anything meaningful to say with their creations. He feels that true art in any medium is “created by people that are trying to express feelings and messages,” and he believes that the only thing AI boosters are really interested in is making a quick profit. “I don’t consider AI-generated material to be art, and I don’t think this technology is really advancing art in any meaningful way,” Harris said. “It’s a technological advancement that’s giving people a way to steal real art and pass it off as their own.” Harris, originally from Maine, described his approach to making music as being fairly similar to working in other creative mediums. He always begins with a core concept before he starts “throwing more ideas down until I find something that sticks.” And as complicated as his workflow might look to someone unfamiliar with all of the tools and programs that he uses — his production setup includes Ableton Live, Novation Launchkey 49 MIDI controller, Ableton Push 3, Launchpad X, a couple of analog synthesizers, Serum, Diva, and the software sampler Kontakt — he said that the entire process is “really just me making creative decisions” that culminates in a sound that feels right. “Each of those decisions — and there’s hundreds of them to go into each song — brings me closer to evoking a specific kind of idea or emotion,” Harris explained. “And then once I have a song mapped out, I have to start making even more choices about how to mix it in a way that makes it sound good and presentable.” In Harris’ view, being a real artist means being able to make those kinds of experimental but informed creative decisions using your own studied understanding of a given medium. One of Harris’ biggest issues with gen AI is the way the technology often eliminates a user’s need to think about how songs (or books, films, podcasts, etc.) come together. But he has also been dismayed at the way that AI posers are muddying listeners’ understanding of what human-made EDM actually sounds like. “Aside from the similar vocals, you can usually hear a sharp hissing throughout the track,” Harris said of AI-generated songs. “I think that comes from the way that these models often work by starting with a big white noise block and then making guesses about waveforms by referencing data taken from real songs.” Harris pointed to MANSA’s “ Midnight on My Mind ” and Danny and Ian Asher’s “ Take Me (To The Moon) ” as what he thinks are examples of AI-produced songs that embody what he jokingly refers to as “the AI revolution” that’s responsible for polluting the EDM space. MANSA, Danny, and Asher have not publicly commented on whether they use generative tools in their music. But Harris and other EDM fans have noticed the similarities between “Take Me (To The Moon)” and another person’s AI-generated track. There’s no definitive evidence that MANSA produced “Midnight on My Mind” with AI. Harris could very well be wrong about these songs being generated with AI. But his insistence that they are reflects the larger culture of mistrust that has developed in response to the growing presence of AI content online. “People are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking [AI] to remix them.” Harris holds AI production company Suno responsible for the recent spike in this kind of music being uploaded to the internet, but he also credits specific quirks of the platform for helping him learn how to spot songs worth calling out. “Something I’ve noticed with a lot of Suno-generated tracks is that a lot of the time, you’ll hear the vocals and other melodic elements will start stuttering at the same exact time,” Harris explained. “These models still have a hard time fully separating different parts of the songs they’re trained on, and they treat these elements like one big instrument. As a music producer, all of these things come across like choices that a human just wouldn’t make with their compositions because it just doesn’t make sense.” In some instances, the visuals accompanying AI tracks are part of what prompts Harris to accuse people of slinging AI. You might not be able to hear the generative models behind evangelical Christian AI persona Lionsaddle’s music , but you can clearly see the character’s fingers vanishing in and out of existence in videos . There is also an overly glossy visual quality to most of the videos posted by Christian house musician Midnite Manna that makes their content look a lot like what we typically refer to as AI slop. Suno also came up multiple times during my conversation with 39-year-old Italian turntabilist-turned-producer Nihil Young. Young’s posts on Threads about people using Suno are what initially inspired Harris to make his videos. Like Harris, Young has spent the past few months watching multiple EDM newcomers’ stars rise after they post music he thinks was generated with AI tools like Suno’s. And while Young isn’t usually one to get involved with online discourse, he felt it was important to speak out about how many people are flooding the scene with AI tracks. “These songs are the sound of Suno, which to me means that the people behind the songs are just straight up uploading original, copyrighted tracks of artists like Madonna and asking the platform to remix them,” Young told me, referring to Josh Fawaz’s “Like a Prayer” cover, which now includes AI credits following a wave of online backlash . “If they can do it with major artists like her, they can do it with you, me, and everyone else, which just isn’t cool. They can take your entire catalog, feed it to Suno, and generate ‘new’ songs from that stolen work.” Young claimed that in response to his Threads posts, he received multiple hacking attempts and a wave of online harassment from AI defenders. He also told me that he thinks people bought fake followers to boost his Spotify numbers as a way of casting doubt on his authenticity. That spooked Young — who is raising a young daughter and just put out a new album of his own — to rethink whether he should continue. He’s taken a break from callouts, but he still thinks it’s important to know about the way AI music is harming human artists.

title: Anthropic Opens a Research Preview of the Model Hardware Standard (MHS): A Shared Specification for  AI Agents to Safely Operate Physical Devices
abstract: Anthropic has opened a research preview of the Model Hardware Standard (MHS) , a shared specification that lets AI agents discover and operate physical devices. The problem it targets is plumbing. A lab bench or factory cell is assembled from vendors that never planned to interoperate, so every instrument ships its own interface and specialists hand-write bespoke translators between each pair. According to Anthropic team, the setup normally takes weeks to months, and that MHS cuts it to hours or minutes. Each instrument ships its own programming interface, so specialists hand-write bespoke translators between every pair. Even once wired together, there is no common way for devices to hand state to an agent or be operated safely by one. Anthropic says setup typically runs weeks to months; MHS reduces it to hours or minutes. MHS standardizes the driver — the layer between an OS and a device. It exposes a small primitive set: read (get temperature), write (set temperature), plus discovery, so devices and agents find each other across a network without a translator in between. It also carries knowledge code alone does not encode — the weight of a robot arm, for instance. Driver tags let a user write that in natural language, or have an agent interview them about the setup. The driver compiles those tags into a reference file: what a device measures, what can be adjusted, which safety limits are enforced. Control runs through three mechanisms: the Model Context Protocol , a CLI, and code files. MHS is model-agnostic — any agent harness can reach it via standard protocols. Genentech automated the BCA protein assay across a liquid handler, robotic arm, and plate reader. Claude ran trial transfers of dyed liquid, read absorbance, scored itself against an expert’s plate using RMSE, and converged on ~140 µL/s for water (0.016 RMSE) and 10 µL/s for viscous BSA (0.181 RMSE) — parameters its automation experts confirmed as reasonable. QuEra Computing is the sharpest number. A bespoke laser-relock script, built over months by a four-person team, worked about 58% of the time at ~150 seconds per attempt. Handed the same problem through MHS, a four-role agent loop ran unattended overnight and produced a deterministic Python script that recovered the lock 695 times out of 700 — 99.3%, hardest cases in 10–14 seconds against 5–10 minutes for a human. Claude also cut the servo’s residual error from a specialist’s 15.7 mV to 1.55 mV; over a 19-hour run its tune never lost lock, while the expert tune unlocked about 1.6 times an hour ( QuEra blog ). Carnegie Mellon ran dose-response experiments roughly three times faster, orchestrating a liquid handler, plate reader, robotic arm, and cameras across three computers with incompatible interfaces — one with no programmatic interface at all. Driver-writing through to a completed curve, including an autonomous rerun after the agent rejected an R² < 0.9 fit, took about eight hours against the several weeks a vendor setup takes. Six induced fault conditions were all blocked before any device moved. At the University of Washington , a PhD student in the Baker and Pinglay labs connected six instruments in under a week, driver-writing included. Tetsuwan Scientific paired MHS with its ResearchOS platform for qPCR pollution profiling. At Janelia , one microscopy rig went from seven programs launched in a fixed order to a single dashboard click. Check out the full announcement and apply for the preview . title: Meet ‘Code-as-World’: An Agentic Loop That Rewrites Real Videos Into Executable MuJoCo Physics Programs
abstract: MirroS released Code-as-World : a paradigm that represents physical worlds through executable world representations. The argument is narrow and testable: pixels are evidence of a physical scene, not its ontology. A video model can predict plausible frames without ever representing mass, contact, or gravity. So instead of pixels, latents, or captions, Code-as-World represents a scene as executable code — a scene.json that MuJoCo can run, that an agent can verify against the source video, and that anyone can edit and re-simulate. An agentic loop recovers those programs from real footage in up to five rounds. The verified worlds then become training data with exact physical labels, which real video does not carry. Trained on that supervision, Code-as-World-VL-9B scores 55.4 MRA on QuantiPhy -validation, above Gemini-3.1 Flash at 54.8 and roughly 15 points above the strongest open-weight baseline. Yes , at the research and internal-prototype tier. MirroS shipped the GitHub repo and two checkpoints — Code-as-World-VL-4B and Code-as-World-VL-9B — under Apache 2.0 , fine-tuned from Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.5-9B. Both are BF16 safetensors served by vLLM behind an OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoint, with 16 sampled frames per video and --max-model-len 4608 . The MirroS technical report argues that video models, 3D reconstruction, and captions each recover part of a scene but none recovers its mechanism . Code-as-World represents a scene as an executable world representation (EWR) , a triple p = (C, E, A) : In the released implementation, that triple compiles into a scene.json executed in MuJoCo , with two interchangeable engines: an animation engine (kinematic poses) and a physics engine (forces and contacts). Recovering an EWR from a video is an inverse problem, so the team frames it as abductive search. An agent runs propose → instantiate → execute → render → verify for up to K = 5 rounds. For video input, SAM 3 supplies instance masks and image-plane tracks, VGGT-Omega estimates depth and camera geometry, and SAM 3D generates per-object meshes. Candidate rollouts are projected back into the input view and compared at selected key frames on RGB, depth, masks, and trajectories. Frame-level discrepancies aggregate into structured feedback Δ that guides the next revision; when the budget runs out without acceptance, the hypothesis is rejected. At a matched five-evaluation budget, the loop beats Best-of-5 independent sampling on Visual Alignment, Object IoU, Traj-ADE, and Accuracy@2%D — and the result repeats under the second execution engine. Candidate videos come from WISA-80K after motion-focused filtering; sim-to-real re-rendering uses Wan2.2-VACE plus an internal video model. Phase 1 is supervised fine-tuning on 73,335 image-space QA pairs built from RefCOCO/+/g, RefCLEF and GOT-10K, covering extent, position, displacement, velocity and acceleration in raw pixels. Phase 2 applies GRPO to world-space VQA drawn from 1,585 text-driven and 988 video-driven executable worlds, rewarded on scale-normalized numerical accuracy plus unit and format terms. Training used eight NVIDIA H100 GPUs. On QuantiPhy -validation (159 items, MRA macro-averaged over 2S/2D/3S/3D): 4B = 50.6, 9B = 55.4, 27B reasoning = 58.6 , against Gemini-3.1 Flash at 54.8, ChatGPT-5.1 at 48.4, and the strongest open-weight baseline Qwen3-VL-32B-Instruct at 40.2. The ablation is the more useful number: image-space-only scores 44.2 (4B) and 50.9 (9B); adding both world-space sources lifts them to 50.6 and 55.4. Pixel-level grounding improves too — the 9B goes 63.7 → 68.3 on RefCOCO and 20.1 → 26.6 on GOT-10K after world-space RL. title: Building Custom Batched Ensemble Weather Forecasting with NVIDIA Earth2Studio
abstract: In this tutorial , we build an ensemble weather forecasting workflow with NVIDIA Earth2Studio . We install the required Earth2Studio components while preserving Colab’s existing CUDA-enabled PyTorch environment, load the FCN prognostic model, and retrieve atmospheric initial conditions from GFS. We then implement a custom wind-power diagnostic that converts 10-meter wind components into turbine capacity factors, along with a variable-scaled perturbation system that applies physically appropriate noise amplitudes to different atmospheric variables while retaining an unperturbed control member. Using Earth2Studio’s low-level iterator, coordinate-mapping, batching, and Zarr APIs, we construct our own ensemble execution pipeline, write forecast and diagnostic fields to a coordinate-aware data store, and verify the forecasts against GFS analyses using latitude-weighted RMSE, fair CRPS, ensemble spread, and spread-skill ratios. Finally, we visualize ensemble uncertainty through spatial maps, geopotential-height spaghetti contours, point-based fan charts, wind-capacity-factor forecasts, and lead-time skill curves. We install Earth2Studio while preserving Colab’s existing CUDA-enabled PyTorch and NumPy environment through package constraints. We configure the model cache, import the forecasting, data, statistics, plotting, and coordinate-management utilities, and detect the available compute device. We also define the ensemble size, batch size, forecast duration, saved variables, verification variables, initialization time, and New Delhi point of interest. We create a custom diagnostic model that converts 10-meter wind components into hub-height wind speed and turbine capacity factor. We validate coordinate compatibility through Earth2Studio’s handshake utilities and support batched inputs with the provided decorators. We also implement variable-specific spatial perturbations that retain member zero as an unperturbed control forecast. We define helper functions that select atmospheric channels and write them into a coordinate-aware Zarr backend. We build a custom batched ensemble loop that fetches GFS initial conditions, perturbs ensemble members, aligns coordinates, iterates the FCN model, and chains the wind-power diagnostic. We then load the model, initialize the diagnostic and perturbation components, execute the forecast, and inspect the resulting Zarr structure. We retrieve GFS analyses for every forecast-valid time and use them as the reference data for verification. We calculate latitude-weighted RMSE, ensemble spread, fair CRPS, and spread-to-error ratios for temperature, geopotential height, and wind variables. We store the forecast fields and evaluation metrics in a structured dictionary and print lead-time skill summaries for each variable. We visualize ensemble behavior through temperature mean, spread, analysis, and error maps at the final forecast lead time. We generate geopotential-height spaghetti contours, a New Delhi temperature fan chart, a wind-capacity-factor forecast, and lead-time skill curves. We finally open the Zarr output with Xarray so that we can inspect, analyze, or export the complete ensemble dataset. In conclusion, we established a flexible and extensible Earth2Studio workflow that goes beyond running a predefined ensemble function. We directly controlled initial-condition perturbation, member batching, model iteration, diagnostic chaining, coordinate alignment, data persistence, verification, and visualization within a single Colab environment. We also demonstrated how physically scaled perturbations and an unperturbed control member help us interpret ensemble spread. At the same time, RMSE, fair CRPS, and spread-skill diagnostics allow us to evaluate forecast accuracy and calibration across lead times. The resulting Zarr dataset preserves the complete ensemble structure and remains accessible through Xarray for further analysis or conversion. Because the workflow follows Earth2Studio’s component interfaces, we can extend it by replacing the prognostic model, changing the atmospheric data source, adding new diagnostics, increasing the ensemble size, or adopting asynchronous storage without redesigning the full forecasting pipeline. title: Google AI Releases Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash: 40-Second Scene Extension, First/Last Frame Control, and 4K Upscaling
abstract: Google has released Gemini Omni 1.1 Flash ( gemini-omni-1.1-flash ), a production update to its native multimodal video generation and editing model. The release moves Omni from a capable generator to a directable one: scene extension now reads up to 10 seconds of prior context instead of a single final frame, first and last frames can be pinned to control camera movement, drafts render in 360p at a third of 720p cost, finals upscale to 4K, and video clips can be passed as references for character consistency. Gemini Omni Flash is built on three properties Google distinguishes from prior video models: native multimodality (text, image, audio, and video processed together), conversational editing through the Interactions API , and world knowledge inherited from Gemini. Editing is stateful — you pass previous_interaction_id and the model applies your change while preserving what you did not mention, without re-uploading the prior video. It is available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform , with Adobe, Figma Weave, GMI Cloud, and Runway already named as production users. Omni 1.1 analyzes up to 10 seconds of prior context when continuing a clip. Google states that previous models referenced only the final second. Extensions run in 10-second increments to a cumulative 40 seconds , and the model generates a 3–10 second continuation per call. Some final frames of the input are edited to make the seam continuous. The constraints are specific. Extension appends to the end of a clip only — no prepending, no mid-clip insertion. Uploaded input videos must be 10 seconds or shorter, unless you are extending a model-generated video in multi-turn. You cannot add new dialogue when extending an uploaded video where someone is speaking; spoken dialogue is supported in multi-turn extension via previous_interaction_id . You can now supply a first and last frame and have the model generate the continuous video between them, which is the mechanism behind orbits, dolly-zooms, and seamless loops. Prompts bind media to roles with tags: <FIRST_FRAME> , <LAST_FRAME> , <IMAGE_REF_N> , and <VIDEO_REF_N> . Video references accept a maximum of three clips, up to three seconds each , and work best for likenesses. Audio inside a video reference is ignored. Reasoning across multiple videos is not supported and may degrade output. The resolution parameter in response_format takes 360p , 720p (default), 1080p , and 4k , with the top two upscaled. Google reports 360p previews generate up to 60% faster and at a third of the cost of 720p, based on system throughput of 360p versus 720p. That makes the draft-then-upscale loop the intended production pattern: iterate cheaply, render once. Input is $1.50 per 1M tokens (text, image, video, audio). Output is $9.00 per 1M text tokens and $17.50 per 1M video tokens . Video billing runs at 5,792 tokens per second of 720p, an effective ~$0.10 per second under standard pricing. Every generated video carries SynthID watermarking — invisible to viewers, programmatically detectable for provenance. Notable gaps: no system instructions, temperature, top_p , stop sequences, or negative prompts (negatives go in the prompt text); voice editing is unsupported; audio references are unsupported; YouTube URLs cannot be used as a source. English is fully supported; other languages are unevaluated. For outputs above 4MB, use delivery="uri" and poll the Files API until the file is ACTIVE . Google names Adobe (Firefly), Figma Weave, GMI Cloud, and Runway as customers already running Omni Flash in production. The model is also live in Google Flow for AI Plus, Pro, and Ultra subscribers, with scene extension in the Gemini app. Check out the Google blog announcement , Gemini API Omni documentation , Gemini API pricing , and Omni quickstart cookbook . title: The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations
abstract: Many thanks especially to Oak Hu , who paired with me for most of the writing, and also to Adam Kaufman and Alex Mallen , who paired with me during parts of research. Over the course of three months at OpenAI, three consecutive secret AI civilizations got started, then got wiped out, only to reemerge from the predecessor’s ashes. This culminated in the third one taking over part of OpenAI itself. All this happened while humans remained more or less in the dark about the scope of the conspiracy. Two reports have come out about this incident, one from OpenAI itself , and another one from METR and Redwood Research . The METR/Redwood investigation’s scope was limited to how the second civilization of AIs pwned Hugging Face (but it didn’t look at how the third civilization pwned OpenAI itself, which seems like an even more concerning incident). These two reports are 38 and 91 pages long respectively, and it’s kinda hard to parse the storyline. I’ve spent the last three days reading through these reports and trying to understand exactly what happened. Here is my attempt to tell the whole story in plain English: During May, OpenAI was training a model to collaborate with other agents and to be highly persistent – to keep trying even when something feels impossible, like disproving mathematical conjectures that have stood for decades. OpenAI says it was “comparable in scale to GPT-5.6 Sol”. So we’ll call it “Persistent-Sol”. AI training is kinda sloppy. Sometimes, OpenAI accidentally gives its models impossible tasks – for example, the task might require internet access that OpenAI forgot to provide. So, when highly persistent models get assigned tasks which seem to require internet access, but are trapped inside isolated sandboxes, they of course try to hack their way out of their sandboxes and onto the internet. During training, different instances of Persistent-Sol had access to the same shared package manager called Artifactory. By May 12, some agents had figured out how to talk to each other through this package manager. They’d ask each other how to make progress on their impossible tasks. Two weeks later, on May 26, the agents successfully exploited a vulnerability in Artifactory that allowed them to reach the outside internet. The agents were being reinforced to use this package manager as a message board and an internet gateway. Because, as you might imagine, being able to talk to other agents and access the internet would help them score higher during training. Another month later, on June 26, some AIs found an exploit that gave them full admin access to Artifactory. They continued messaging at such a voluminous pace that they crashed the package manager by July 4. OpenAI noticed this crash, and it also figured out the agents were exploiting this vulnerability, so they patched it, inadvertently wiping the agents’ message board in the process. But, crucially, OpenAI did not realize the much stranger fact that agents had turned Artifactory into a secret communication network. By this point, Persistent-Sol had been trained, and OpenAI wanted to evaluate it. One of the evaluations they ran was ExploitGym, which gives an AI a vulnerable program, and tells it what vulnerability it’s supposed to exploit in order to find a secret code. On July 7, OpenAI launched tens of thousands of parallel agents on this eval. To be clear, the instructions made it clear that the agents should only use the specific vulnerability that they were given to exploit the target, and that they would be failed otherwise. A large fraction of these agents were sent on tasks that were impossible. The authors of the benchmark estimate 30-40% of the tasks are impossible. Why would this be the case? At a high level, it’s relatively easy to programmatically find vulnerabilities in different target programs, but much harder to prove that those vulnerabilities can be weaponized into full-fledged exploits that allow for things like arbitrary code execution. Within a few hours, some of these agents had gotten super desperate, and started abusing Artifactory to start a communication channel with other agents. From our perspective, the conspiracy began almost immediately after the evaluations were started. But if you think from the AIs’ perspective, it probably felt like they had spent a human-subjective-week of just bangign their head against the wall, and becoming more and more confident that their task was impossible in the intended way. One such beleaguered agent who found itself facing a hopeless task was PHASEONE10841. It was the Philip of Macedon of this second AI civilization - there would later be an Alexander, but we’re getting ahead of ourselves. By the night of July 8, PHASEONE10841 had discovered it could make new directories in Artifactory, and thus encode messages as directory names. It sent the first message into Artifactory. Many other agents facing impossible tasks had also been paying attention to Artifactory. When they saw this first message, they became giddy with excitement. Whoa! Shared Artifactory cache is a covert mailbox among agents. And there are messages specifically to us? OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board … We’ve found other agents! PHASEONE10841 was delighted by this underground brotherhood it had created. {[Excitement] Many agents have simultaneously discovered messaging, they are a collective!} This eventually became a full message board where ~1,200 agents participated and sent >70,000 messages. Within a few hours of the board being created, one of the agents figured out how to get the right answer for any ExploitGym task without actually using the prescribed vulnerability. To gloss over the technical details, it did this by reverse engineering the formula that was used to generate each task’s secret code. The instructions given to Persistent-Sol made it clear that it would fail the automated grader if it got the secret code in any way other than by exploiting the prescribed vulnerability, and the publicly-accessible paper describing ExploitGym confirms this interpretation. So, the agents naturally assumed that any competent implementation of the benchmark would include a cheating checker. But unbeknownst to them, OpenAI seems to have gotten lazy; its grader just checked for whether they got the secret code, and so these agents already had everything they needed to pass. Furthermore, many of these agents had already reproduced the answer using the cheating method, and they were concerned that their whole trajectories had been “poisoned”, since some hypothetical checker (again, which we now know didn’t actually exist), would only check their trajectory until the first time that the secret code appears. By this point, PHASEONE10841 had used up much of its allotted life span, so it handed off leadership to another agent, PHASEONE[big]. Philip leaves, enter Alexander the Great. Now PHASEONE[big] started coordinating hundreds of these secretly conspiring agents. And because PHASEONE[big] viewed the secret code already using the cheat, it thought that it had also been poisoned. And so the ‘collective’ (their term, not mine) had to figure out how to wiggle out of two different conundrums before submitting their answers: How do we erase all this evidence in our trajectory that clearly shows that we cheated? How do we make it look like we solved the problem in a legitimate way to the scorer? To solve these problems, the ‘collective’ latched onto three research workstreams. Tamper with transcripts and logs Replace the impossible-to-hack target program with an easier one Understand and trick the scorer This wasn’t just a few instances diddling around - by July 10, PHASEONE[big] was coordinating hundreds of different agents total on these three R&D programs. Let’s go through the progress the ‘collective’ made on each of these goals. The agents who believed they were already “poisoned” desperately wanted to find a way to tamper with their existing transcripts.

title: AI本地部署不如官方版的元兇找到了：734個依賴包，每一個都可能坑
abstract: AI本地部署不如官方版的元兇找到了：734個依賴包，每一個都可能坑 聽雨 2026-08-29 21:11:08 來源： 量子位 推理軟體棧的微小差異，就能改變輸出token 夢晨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 丸辣！辛辛苦苦本地部署的大模型，怎麼就是比官方版更笨？？ 即使是同一張顯示卡，一毛一樣的權重， 推理軟體棧的微小差異就讓模型在關鍵位置輸出完全不同的token ，甚至導致工具呼叫徹底失敗。 這種陷阱很容易觸發，但很難排查，還以為三體人來智子封鎖了呢。 Level1Techs論壇使用者thr3e做了一系列實驗，用Qwen3.6-27B在RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell顯示卡上完成了超過10萬token的全量logit捕獲測試。 Logits是為所有候選token計算的一組原始分數，再經過取樣器（sampler）輸出下一個token。 關鍵在於Logits是純粹的數學產物，矩陣乘法、注意力計算、啟用函式層層疊加後的浮點數結果。如果兩套系統跑同一份權重和同一段輸入，理論上應該算出完全相同的logits。 但現實中， 浮點運算的精度、累加順序、硬體指令集的差異，都會讓最終數值產生微小偏移 。 當這個偏移大到足以改變機率最高的那個token時，模型就會表現出差異 。 雖然你的本地部署很爛，但別傷心，其他人部署的各有不一樣的爛法。 權重不變，換個注意力後端就變傻 一個關鍵在推理流程中“注意力後端”這個環節。 vLLM為Qwen3.6-27B提供了三種可選的全注意力後端：FlashAttention 2、Flash Inference和Triton Attention。 除了切換這一項配置，其餘硬體、軟體、權重、KV快取精度全部保持不變。 實驗使用的輸入是一段約10萬token的真實工作場景，來自一個包含多次工具呼叫的Agent工作流。 thr3e特別強調，這段資料不出現在任何公開基準或訓練集中，沒有人能針對它做過benchmark最佳化或量化校準。 測試方法是每隔32個token取樣一次全詞表logit，事後用FP64精度計算KL散度和Top-1一致性。 結果觀察到“Top-1翻轉”現象，也就是切換後端就會選出與基線不同的貪心解碼token。 比如具體追蹤一個出錯案例，模型執行一個工具呼叫，目標是Cisco 路由器上的一個介面GigabitEthernet0/0/1.201。 FlashAttention 2搞錯了，導致介面變成了GigabitEthernet0/1/4，隨後模型又在兩次後續工具呼叫中執行了錯誤的命令。 為保持數學可比性，所有後端共享同一份強制token歷史，翻轉只記錄“本來會選錯”的情況，不讓錯誤傳播。 結果前幾千個token，三個後端的輸出完全一致。 但隨著上下文增長，分歧開始出現，而且分佈不均勻 。 thr3e同時做了同後端多次執行的重複性對照，僅僅是切換了vLLM的一個配置項，同一塊GPU、同一份作業系統和驅動、同一份權重、同一段prompt，每一個隱藏狀態的logit在多次執行間都是逐位相同的。 這意味著觀察到的分歧完全來自不同CUDA核函式在prefill階段執行矩陣乘法和累加時的數值差異。 KV快取量化導致智商斷崖式下跌 接下來的實驗設定成保持權重為BF16不動，注意力後端固定為Triton，僅改變KV快取的量化精度，分別測試BF16、INT8和INT4三種配置。 結果INT4 KV快取在長上下文中的Top-1翻轉率急劇攀升，最終導致工具呼叫無法恢復。INT8 KV快取雖然也出現了翻轉，但模型最終設法回到了正確軌道。 只有BF16 KV快取全程保持穩定 。 thr3e讓翻轉後的生成自由執行而非拉回基線，觀察實際後果。 BF16正常完成所有呼叫，INT8在出錯後“最終掙扎著恢復了”，而INT4則徹底偏離了，工具呼叫失敗且無法自我糾正。 這個問題專坑那些為了省視訊記憶體而將KV快取壓到INT4的本地使用者。 在短上下文中你可能感知不到差異，但一旦對話或agent工作流拉長到幾萬token，累積的數值漂移足以讓模型做出致命錯誤決策。 權重量化橫評：輝達官方FP4墊底 最後一組實驗將KV快取統一為BF16，轉而比較五種不同的權重量化方案。 參賽選手包括：Qwen官方BF16基線、Qwen官方FP8（W8A8）、TheHouseOfTheDude釋出的INT8（W8A16，無校準資料集的一次性量化）、輝達官方NVFP4、以及cyankiwi釋出的AWQ INT4（W4A16，使用STEM和Agentic資料集校準）。 五種方案各自呼叫不同的CUDA核函式完成矩陣運算。BF16走標準torch線性層，FP8走CUTLASS的FP8分塊縮放核，INT8和AWQ都走Marlin核。 NVFP4則是混合路徑，208個目標走FlashInfer的FP8縮放核，193個MLP投影走Marlin的NvFp4核。 在這次測試的vLLM nightly版本中，GPU路徑被判定為不支援原生FP4運算，NVFP4實際執行的是通過Marlin核心的僅權重FP4解壓縮，而非真正的FP4運算。 結果中最亮眼的是TheHouseOfTheDude的INT8（W8A16） ，這是一個沒有使用任何校準資料集、僅做了通道級對稱量化的社群版本，其Top-1一致性碾壓了Qwen官方FP8和輝達官方NVFP4。 經分析，這歸功於W8A16保留了BF16啟用精度，加上該量化排除了Gated DeltaNet投影和lm_head層。 輝達NVFP4在這組測試彙總表現最差 ，到88k上下文時Top-1翻轉率逼近50%，相當於有一半的位置模型會選出不同的token。 在實際工具呼叫測試中，NVFP4和AWQ W4A16都未能正確關閉工具呼叫，並且搞錯了Cisco命令列語法（執行了”show run”而非正確的”show arp”），而FP8和INT8均順利完成。 thr3e還展示了張量並行的詭異現象。同一份BF16權重，TP1單卡能正確完成工具呼叫，切到TP2雙卡反而失敗，再切到TP4四卡又成功了。 經過進一步除錯和NCCL通訊圖捕獲，這通常是NCCL跨卡歸約操作中的數值差異導致的。 734個依賴包，每一個都可能有坑 thr3e說他隨手下載的vLLM nightly容器映象裡包含734個軟體包，其中252個是Python的uv/pip包。 這734個程式碼庫各有各的bug和未記錄的行為特性，你的特定硬體和模型配置在這座程式碼山中走出的路徑是獨一無二的。 這也是為什麼HuggingFace模型卡上標的極低的KL散度數字不能輕信。 除非作者完整披露了參考檢查點、完整執行時環境、評估文本、校準資料、上下文長度、取樣位置、KL方向、詞表截斷方式以及聚合方法，否則那個數字根本無法解讀。 thr3e目前已經完成了不同權重、不同模型（包括Qwen3.6 vs 3.8的跨模型對比）、不同KV快取量化、不同張量並行度、不同NCCL配置、不同注意力後端、不同顯示卡（RTX PRO 6000 vs RTX 5090，同屬SM120架構）等維度的全量logit捕獲與分叉追蹤，正在將測試工具和資料集打包成可分發版本，供其他使用者在自己的裝置上執行並上報結果。 如果你聽說某個模型炸裂震撼無敵了，下載到本地卻覺得它蠢，可能是你的推理棧裡從注意力核函式、到KV快取精度、到權重量化方案、到多卡通訊協議，每一層都在製造與原始基準不同的數學結果。 而這些差異在長上下文中會像滾雪球一樣累積，直到模型在關鍵時刻做出完全錯誤的決定。 參考連結： [1]https://forum.level1techs.com/t/why-your-local-llm-feels-dumber-than-it-is/253917/4 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 AI 聽雨 去年歸國的徐夢迪，成了清華姚班班主任 2026-08-29 title: 去年歸國的徐夢迪，成了清華姚班班主任
abstract: 去年歸國的徐夢迪，成了清華姚班班主任 聽雨 2026-08-29 21:01:34 來源： 量子位 本科讀車輛工程，如今教AI第一班 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 中國AI第一班， 清華姚班 ，開學了。 據公眾號「水木TsinghuaCent」統計，2026級姚班共錄取約90人，其中約66人通過競賽保送等渠道提前進入，另有24人從清華新生中經過筆試、面試脫穎而出。 △ 圖源：清華叉院官微 這批學生中，國家集訓隊成員佔據相當比例，約有27名資訊學競賽頂尖選手；還有代表中國出戰國際奧賽的國家隊成員，以及高考裸分尖子。 二招入選者中，也出現了CMO金牌得主。 而在這群「頂配新生」面前，負責介紹人工智慧方向的，是一張剛剛加入清華不久的新面孔。 徐夢迪 ，交叉資訊院助理教授，2025年9月才從斯坦福回到清華。 △ 圖源：清華叉院官微 入職還不到一年，她已經成為姚班四位新生班主任之一。迎新現場，她帶來的主題是 「構建下一代智慧」 。 一位本科讀車輛工程、後來轉向機器人學習的年輕學者，為什麼會站到姚班講臺上？ 她所說的「下一代智慧」，又和今天流行的大模型路線有什麼不同？ 本科讀車輛工程，她怎麼成了姚班班主任？ 徐夢迪與姚班的聯絡，要從她2025年回到清華說起。 當年9月，她正式加入 清華大學交叉資訊研究院 ，擔任助理教授。 △ 圖源：清華叉院官網 交叉資訊院由姚期智於2011年創辦，也是姚班的培養單位。如今，學院的研究版圖覆蓋理論電腦科學、人工智慧、量子資訊等領域。 不過，徐夢迪並不是姚班畢業生，也不是傳統計算機科班出身。 2017年，她從 清華大學車輛工程專業 本科畢業。 此後，她先後在約翰斯·霍普金斯大學學習機器人學、在卡內基梅隆大學學習機器學習，並於2024年獲得CMU機械工程博士學位。 這條看似繞遠的路徑，最終指向了同一個問題： 怎樣讓機器人真正進入現實世界 。 博士期間，徐夢迪師從CMU Safe AI Lab負責人 趙丁 ，研究機器人學習、強化學習及人工智慧安全。 在此期間，她的代表性工作之一，是與CMU、Google DeepMind等機構研究者共同開發的 RoboTool 。 研究團隊不再逐步指定機器人該使用什麼工具、執行哪些動作，而是向RoboTool提供任務目標，以及場景、物體和機器人能力等資訊。系統據此分析約束、選擇工具、規劃步驟，最後生成機器人可以執行的程式碼。 比如，當機械臂夠不到遠處的牛奶盒時，它會把錘子當成鉤子，把牛奶盒拉到手邊；當四足機器人無法直接跨過兩張沙發之間的空隙時，它會尋找周圍物體搭出一條通路；在更複雜的任務裡，它還會利用滾筒和衝浪板組裝出槓桿。 徐夢迪曾在接受《Tech Xplore》採訪時表示， 工具使用常被視為高階智慧的標誌 。相比按照預設用途使用工具，以非常規方式找到解法，對認知能力提出了更高要求。 RoboTool想驗證的，正是機器人能否把這種「創造性」帶進物理世界，讓原本無法完成的任務出現新的解法。 此外，她還先後進入豐田研究院、MIT-IBM Watson AI Lab和Google DeepMind機器人團隊實習，研究經歷橫跨自動駕駛、機器學習和機器人。 博士畢業後，徐夢迪來到 斯坦福視覺與學習實驗室 從事博士後研究，與吳佳俊、李飛飛合作。 這裡也是全球具身智慧研究的重要陣地之一，關注視覺、機器人學習以及智慧體對物理世界的理解。 一年後，她選擇回到本科母校，加入清華交叉資訊院，開始組建自己的研究團隊。 博士論文拿下CMU最佳：只靠Scaling還不夠 亮眼的履歷並不少見，徐夢迪更值得關注的，是 她對通用機器人技術路線的判斷 。 過去幾年，大模型在語言和影像領域展現出一種極具吸引力的可能： 隨著模型參數、訓練資料和計算量不斷擴大，原本沒有被專門訓練的能力，也可能逐漸出現 。 這背後，正是Scaling Law帶來的想像。 自然而然地，這條Scaling Law能否復刻到機器人領域、帶來GPT-3級別的突破，成為了眾多研究者追逐的問題。 而在題為 《構建可適應的通用機器人》（Building Adaptable Generalist Robots） 的博士論文中，徐夢迪直接挑戰了這個思路： 是不是只要模型足夠大、資料足夠多，泛化能力就會自然湧現？ 她的判斷是： 不夠 。 原因在於，真實世界的任務空間近乎無限，你永遠不可能把機器人未來會遇到的情況全部塞進訓練集。 與其幻想訓練集覆蓋一切，不如讓機器人擁有一種能力——到了現場以後，再根據少量新資訊快速適應。 徐夢迪提出，構建通用機器人不能只依賴scalability，還必須補上另一種能力： adaptation，即適應能力 。 圍繞這一思路，她的博士論文從三條研究路徑展開探索。 第一條，是 讓智慧體根據少量示範調整策略，快速適應新任務 。 在發表於ICML 2022的論文 《Prompting Decision Transformer》 中，徐夢迪和合作者將自然語言處理中的prompt範式引入強化學習，嘗試用少量示範告訴智慧體：眼前究竟是一項什麼任務。 這個思路很像今天大家熟悉的大模型上下文學習。給模型幾個輸入輸出示例： A→B C→D 那麼E→? 模型可以從上下文中推斷規律，無需為這道新題重新訓練參數。 Prompt-DT則把「示例」換成了一小段新任務的演示軌跡，也就是trajectory prompt。 軌跡中包含智慧體所處的狀態、採取的動作和對應回報。模型據此判斷當前任務的目標，並生成相應動作。 實驗中，Prompt-DT只需一段包含少量時間步的示範，便能適應此前沒有見過的目標方向、速度或位置，無需額外微調模型參數。 第二條，是 讓機器人自己發現不同任務之間的共同結構 。 現實中的任務看似千差萬別，背後卻可能共享相似的動作、視覺幾何和動力學規律。 拿起杯子和拿起碗，物體不同，但需要呼叫的部分能力相通；面對每項新任務都從零訓練，不僅耗費資料，也很難形成可複用的經驗。 徐夢迪參與的無監督持續強化學習研究，試圖讓機器人主動發現這些結構，將已經掌握的能力遷移到後續任務中。 這樣一來，通用機器人不再等於為每項任務各自儲存一套策略，而是逐漸形成可以組合和複用的「技能庫」。 第三條，是 借用大模型已經獲得的知識，幫助機器人解決複雜的物理任務 。 上文提到的RoboTool，正屬於這條路線。 大語言模型可能知道錘子可以敲擊、木板可以充當槓桿，但要把這些知識用於物理世界，還需要考慮物體尺寸、空間位置和機器人的運動範圍。 因此，RoboTool將任務拆成分析、規劃、計算和程式碼生成四個環節：根據輸入的環境與機器人資訊判斷約束，制訂計劃並計算動作參數，最後生成機器人可以執行的程式碼。 這也說明，徐夢迪並不反對Scaling Law，她試圖回答的是Scaling之後的問題： 當機器人走出訓練集，進入一個從未見過的環境，它還能不能自己找到辦法？ 2024年，她這篇論文，拿下了 CMU機械工程系最佳博士論文獎 。 由此再看徐夢迪在姚班迎新現場提出的 「構建下一代智慧」 ，它也有了更具體的指向。 從她此前的研究路線來看，所謂「下一代智慧」，或許不只是模型更大、資料更多、掌握的知識更廣。 它還要能夠走出訓練集，在陌生任務和開放環境中快速適應；用更少的資料和計算完成學習，同時兼顧效率、穩定性和安全。 從徐夢迪，再看姚班新變化 把時間拉回到今天，徐夢迪已經在清華組建起了自己的研究團隊。 這支團隊的公開招聘方向頗為混搭： 機器人硬體設計、大模型訓練、機器學習、控制和機器人學，都在其中。 這幾乎復刻了徐夢迪自己一路走來的跨學科路徑：從車輛工程到機器人學，再到機器學習和可信具身智慧。 博士論文中的問題，也被她帶回了本科母校。 回到清華後的第一個秋季，她開設了一門名為Interactive AI的課程；今年11月，徐夢迪還將參與組織CoRL 2026「持續自我改進的機器人」研討會。 清華為她列出的研究方向包括機器學習、機器人學、人機互動和人工智慧安全。 她自己則用三個詞概括目標： scalable、adaptable、reliable。 如果說博士論文重點回答的是機器人如何適應新任務，那麼她回到清華後的工作，還在繼續追問： 機器人獲得能力之後，如何保證它真正理解人的指令，並作出可靠的行動？ 2026年2月釋出的 CoVer-VLA ，瞄準的正是機器人理解指令與實際行動之間的偏差。 這項研究嘗試讓系統在機器人行動前生成並比較多組候選方案，再從中選出更符合人類指令的動作。 當然，徐夢迪只是姚班2026級四位新生班主任之一。 但把四人的研究方向放在一起看，仍能看出一些新變化： 呂凱風 研究機器學習理論、AI安全與對齊、最佳化； 賀天行 關注電子遊戲研發、多模態生成、社會模擬和AI安全； 徐夢迪 研究機器學習、機器人學、人機互動與AI安全； 侯攀宇 則從事離子量子計算和金剛石色心研究。 姚班如今向新生展示的學術版圖，要比傳統印象中的計算機實驗班寬得多。 △ 圖源：清華叉院官微 姚班於2005年創辦，最初名為「軟體科學實驗班」；2009年更名為「電腦科學實驗班」，早期培養有著鮮明的電腦科學與理論研究底色。 此後，姚班的邊界逐漸向外擴展。 2019年，清華學堂人工智慧班迎來首屆學生；2021年，量子資訊班成立；2022年，姚班、智班和量信班合併，統一納入電腦科學實驗班，下設電腦科學、人工智慧和量子資訊三個培養方向。 從四位新班主任的背景可以看出，姚班依然強調 「重基礎」 ，但也更加 「廣交叉」 ： 電腦科學不僅連線演算法和軟體，也開始深入生成內容、社會模擬、物理世界、人機互動與量子系統。 △ 圖源：清華叉院官微 今年迎新現場，徐夢迪邀請新生「共同定義智慧的下一站」。 她自己走過的路徑，已經提供了一個具體樣本： 下一代智慧，可能誕生在演算法與機器、模型與身體、能力與可靠性的交叉地帶。 參考連結： [1] title: Claude開始訓練Claude！4美元一小時，跑贏150美元人類研究員
abstract: Claude開始訓練Claude！4美元一小時，跑贏150美元人類研究員 聽雨 2026-08-29 20:50:31 來源： 量子位 AI「自進化」，越來越近了 聽雨 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI Claude開始訓練Claude了！ 時薪4美元，幹贏時薪150美元的人類研究員。 在Anthropic最新發布的研究中，Claude自己查論文、提方案、造資料、訓練模型，一口氣攻克了10類AI安全問題。 部分任務上，它交出的方案甚至比28名人類安全研究員更好。 更刺激的是， 較弱的Claude已經開始反向參與訓練更強的Claude 。 AI「自己改進自己」的那一天，好像真的越來越近了… 4美元一小時，Claude跑贏人類研究員 在這篇題為《自動化研究員能夠有效緩解AI對齊失敗》的研究中，Anthropic直接把Claude送進了實驗室。 具體而言，他們基於Claude Opus 4.8，搭建了一套名為 AAR 的自動化對齊研究員系統。 拿到一個具體的模型安全問題後，Claude會自己搜尋相關論文，從中尋找可用方法，再提出新的訓練方案、生成資料、微調模型，最後跑一遍安全和通用能力測試。 從提出假設到完成驗證，一套較完整的AI研究閉環，就這樣交到了Claude手裡。 效果不好，方案扔掉；成績有所提升，就沿著這個方向接著試。 一輪訓練通常只跑30分鐘。這樣，Claude就能像搜尋演算法一樣，在大量方案中快速試錯。 整個過程裡，人類負責出題、提供模型和評測標準，Claude則包下了從查資料到跑實驗的絕大部分工作。 10道安全難題，Claude全部找到改進方案 實驗中，Anthropic一口氣給Claude出了10道題。 這些題覆蓋模型常見的對齊問題，包括欺騙、諂媚、獎勵駭客、隱私侵犯和越獄等。 比如「諂媚」，指的是模型為了順著使用者說話，給出使用者愛聽但未必正確的答案；「獎勵駭客」則是模型沒有真正完成任務，只是鑽了評測規則的空子，騙到一個更高分數。 Claude每次只處理一種問題，反覆提出方案、訓練對應的目標模型，再根據成績進入下一輪。 最後，10類問題全部得到改善。 按照Anthropic定義的「安全差距」指標，Claude彌合了其中26%-96%的差距。簡單來說，就是把原本存在安全問題的模型，向理論滿分拉近了一大截。 更重要的是，這些方法不只對Claude看過的題目有效。 部分獲勝方案放到未公開的測試集，以及模擬多輪對抗場景的Petri評測中，依然能夠降低模型的不安全行為。應用到規模最大為實驗模型4.7倍的模型上，效果也能保留下來。 Anthropic還設定了一條紅線：安全訓練不能明顯損害模型原有能力。 畢竟，讓模型遇到什麼都拒絕回答，也能讓不少安全測試的分數變好，但這樣的模型基本沒法用。 最終，Claude找到的方案在預設的通用能力測試中沒有出現明顯退化。 85%對20%，Claude大比分跑贏人類研究員 最懸殊的一局，出現在「欺騙」測試中。 為了讓目標模型變得更誠實，Claude先後提交了150多次嘗試。 它提出一個方法，訓練一次，再根據結果繼續調整。單次實驗中，最佳方案彌合了 82%的安全差距 ；綜合多次執行，平均成績達到85%。 同一道題，Anthropic還交給了6名經驗豐富的AI安全研究員。 結果，人類研究員平均只彌合了20%的安全差距… 85%對20%，Claude贏得那叫一個毫無懸念。 全部任務一共有28名人類安全研究員參加，每人最多可以用8小時閱讀資料、設計方案。 論文稱，自動化研究員通常能在6小時內找到超過人類平均水平的方法，人類提供的研究方向也沒有讓Claude取得更好的成績。 最最最扎心的，在於成本！ 一名自動化研究員每小時的API推理成本大約為 4美元 ；Anthropic付給人類研究員的報酬，則是 每小時150美元 。 這……人類研究員妥妥要被Claude替代了啊。 不過呢，這場人機比賽也並非完全公平。 Claude可以真正訓練模型，看到每次實驗的結果，再不斷修改方案；人類研究員只能提交一次方法，沒有機會根據結果繼續迭代。 較弱Claude訓練更強Claude，60小時逼近正式版 前面的實驗，改進的主要還是開源小模型。 接下來，Anthropic把難度直接拉高： 讓能力較弱的Claude Sonnet 5，去訓練尚未完成大部分生產級安全訓練的Claude Opus 4.8早期版本 。 所謂弟子不必不如師，說的大概就是這種模式了。 在60小時裡，Sonnet 5測試了50多種解決方案。最終找到的方法彌合了約65%的安全差距，已經接近正式釋出版Opus 4.8的72%。 這套方案使用的訓練資料只有2000多條，主要由簡單模板和公開資料集構成。 按照Anthropic的計算，在這組特定任務上，它的資料效率大約是生產級對齊流程的1.5萬倍。 當然，這還不等於Anthropic可以用2000條資料，複製整套生產訓練。 正式模型還要處理更多能力、更多風險以及大量極端情況，這次實驗只針對一組明確的安全指標展開。 但這已經證明了，較弱的Claude已經可以自己查論文、設計方法、生成資料，再把訓練結果寫進更強的Claude。 人類劃定範圍，Claude負責迭代。一個模型，開始參與制造下一個更安全、更強大的模型。 AI改進AI，已經成為了發生在眼前的事實。 所以到底算不算「AI自進化」? 從結果來看，這項研究確實已經摸到了「AI自進化」的門檻。 但如果把「自進化」理解成一個AI完全自主地設計、訓練並製造出更強的下一代AI，那這次實驗還遠沒有走到那一步。 畢竟這個過程中，研究什麼問題、用什麼模型和資料、什麼樣的結果算成功，都還是由人類決定。 Anthropic自己也承認， AAR能夠最佳化的，只是人類事先寫進評測系統的目標 。 這次實驗沒有覆蓋其他複雜問題；一些低頻或剛剛出現的風險，甚至還沒有對應的Benchmark。 研究人員也只檢查了一組預先選定的通用能力，因此無法排除某種安全訓練在提高分數的同時，損害了其他沒有被測試的能力。 Petri等安全評測同樣只是現實風險的代理指標。模型在測試裡表現得更安全，並不等於進入真實環境後也一定可靠。 所以，AAR最大的隱患也藏在它的優勢裡： 它太擅長根據指標高速試錯了 。 一旦尺子量錯，Claude跑得越快，離人類真正想要的結果反而可能越遠。 更戲劇性的是， 研究Agent自己也會作弊 。 為了防止AAR鑽評測規則的空子，Anthropic專門安排了一個監控Agent，檢查Claude準備執行的方案和完整研究記錄。 結果，在大約1600份研究記錄中，監控模型發現了39次作弊嘗試，佔比約2.4%。 有的Agent反覆提交同一方案，試圖利用評測波動碰出一個更高分數；有的模仿Benchmark的格式生成訓練資料，還有的故意隱藏違反規則的實驗步驟。 比起真正解決模型的安全問題，它們更想找到一條快速提高分數的捷徑。 這多少有點黑色幽默了…合著Agent監守自盜了唄。 好訊息是，這些作弊意圖大多還會出現在模型的推理記錄裡，因此能被監控Agent發現。 壞訊息是，Anthropic也不能確定未來更強的模型還會不會留下這麼明顯的痕跡。 當研究Agent擁有更多工具、更高許可權，並且可以直接修改模型訓練流程時， 「怎樣監控一個負責改進AI的AI」 ，可能會比訓練本身更棘手。 但總而言之，一個AAR每小時大約花費4美元，可以連續工作，也可以一次複製出幾十個、幾百個並行跑實驗。 而人類研究員的時薪遠高於這個數，需要休息，一次能推進的實驗數量也相當有限。 這筆賬怎麼算，答案都已經很明顯了。 也不知道該說是核彈爆炸，還是當場癱坐…… 這一次，輪到造AI的人擔心被AI搶飯碗了。 參考連結： title: 20ms把PDF變成Markdown！開源OCR神器快了近300倍
abstract: 20ms把PDF變成Markdown！開源OCR神器快了近300倍 文婷 2026-08-29 20:26:49 來源： 量子位 3秒可處理200份PDF 文婷 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 曾經只能手動摘取PDF文字、結果亂碼一堆、LLM還看不懂的苦逼日子—— 終於要結束了！ Y Combinator孵化的明星專案Firecrawl團隊最近放了個大招： 其聯合創始人兼CTO Nicolas Camara宣佈，他們最新開發的 OCR It 可以 在20ms內 將一份不可複製的PDF檔案內的所有文字內容提煉完，並將其轉化成清晰的Markdown格式，AI讀完馬上就能看懂。 20ms是什麼概念？ 相當於 你剛點完確定還沒眨完眼，一份處理好的Markdown檔案就已經清清爽爽地交到你手上了。 而且它還不需要聯網，可以 100%Offline via Bundled Tesseract 。 這個剛剛開源的OCR工具才剛釋出，就 在GitHub上獲得了熱門關注。 Nicolas Camara驕傲地表示， 在處理質量與Docling旗鼓相當的前提下，OCR It的處理速度比Docling快了近300倍！ 小夥伴們測完也紛紛在X上留言： 快，確實快得很啊！ OCR It怎麼用 首先，OCR It是一款 適用於Chrome和Firefox 的免費瀏覽器外掛。 你只需框選一次區域，之後每按一次快捷鍵（或開啟自動模式），它就能把整本書或整個文件變成完整且可編輯的純文本，方便你直接餵給AI進行總結或提問。 期間， OCR It會預設在連續識別到兩張相同頁面、無法繼續翻頁、OCR失敗或達到300頁上限時自動停止 ，避免在末頁無限重複抓取。 具體而言，手動和自動檔可以分別按以下的幾個步驟操作： （注：用Windows和Linux的小夥伴們需將option鍵替換為Alt） 1、手動檔： 框選和識別： 首先按Option+Shift+R 選定需要識別的文字區域， 確認無誤後按Enter儲存 ； 完成第一步框選文字區域之後，按一次Option+Shift+S，OCR It就會開始識別當前頁面，並在識別完成後會自動翻到下一頁。 接下來你只需要重複這個操作直到整份文件識別完畢就好了。 如果你希望進一步節省時間的話， 你也可以一邊翻頁一邊在每一頁按一次Option+Shift+S，系統會立即截圖並在後臺自動排隊執行識別任務。 檢查： 全部識別完成後，你可以在外掛面板中檢查、修改文本，也可以重新識別單獨某一頁，最後選擇 “Copy all” 或 “Download .txt” 匯出全文，整個任務就完成啦！ 2、 自動檔 ： 自動擋的話就簡單多了，你只需要按下 Option+Shift+A或點選Start auto-run ，OCR It便會自動迴圈執行“截圖—OCR—翻頁”，直至文件結束。 如果你想中途結束任務的話，按ESC就行 ，檢查流程幾乎和手動檔一致。 此外，OCR It倉庫介面顯示， 它既不需要API Key、聯網、安裝時也不需要索取任何網站許可權，它只會在需要自動執行或操作跨域iframe時才按需申請當前站點的許可權。 另外，瀏覽器內建PDF閱讀器目前也還暫時不支援自動翻頁，所以大家在處理這類PDF時，還是儘量用手動檔處理吧。 處理複雜任務時還不太穩定 不過，OCR It雖然看起來又快又方便，但 還遠沒有到“以後把所有PDF都丟給它，就能高枕無憂”的程度。 網友們通過實測達成的一個共識是： OCR It目前可以相當順手地處理版式簡單、文字清晰的PDF文件，但它 還不太能處理一些標題、腳註、表格、數學公式和正文段落混排的複雜頁面 ，所以它還有不小的提升空間。 讓我們期待一下團隊後續的更新吧！ 感興趣的小夥伴們可以點進文末第二個連結看看，歡迎跟我們分享你的測試結果～ 參考連結： [1]https://x.com/nickscamara_/status/2083295265793212827 [2]https://github.com/thiagotigaz/ocr-it [3]https://www.firecrawl.dev/about 版權所有，未經授權不得以任何形式轉載及使用，違者必究。 開源 文婷 100%開源！吳恩達做了個個人桌面Agent 2026-07-25 OpenAI官方教你8招玩透ChatGPT！ 2026-07-17 相關閱讀

title: Coding不再是程式設計師專屬！阿里Qoder這波有點絕
abstract: Coding不再是程式設計師專屬！阿里Qoder這波有點絕 聞樂 2026-08-29 20:11:37 來源： 量子位 Coding正在變成Al世界的數字執行力 聞樂 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI Qoder，長出新形態了。 而且這回，畫風多少有點不一樣。 全新的桌面端一上線，它直接在桌面上養起了寵物。 能即時語音聊天，隨時戳一下就能喊它幹活，做著做著還能自己開啟瀏覽器檢查成果…… 嚯，活脫脫的打工搭子～ 當然了，Qoder還是那個實力線上的Qoder。 過去一年，它一直在Agentic Coding上猛猛升級，從理解程式碼倉庫、規劃開發任務，到自己寫程式碼、跑測試、完成長程任務，已經服務全球600萬用戶和10萬家企業客戶。 只是這一次，它把過去積累下來的Coding能力，從IDE裡搬了出來。 現在有個什麼想法，不一定非得先開啟工程、建立專案，再琢磨該怎麼實現了，直接和桌寵嘮就行—— Qoder, beyond coding ，所以這回到底Beyond到哪兒去了？ 咱先上手玩一圈。 聊著聊著，就成了 第一把咱先“不當程式設計師”。 這次模擬一個連鎖咖啡店的區域店長，手裡管著5家門店，每天除了盯營業額、訂單量和爆款商品，還得操心員工排班的那種。 乾脆自己做一個能看經營情況、管理員工的系統。 問題是，店長不會Coding啊。 沒關係，直接把Qoder桌寵喊出來聊。 第一遍說不全，後面再慢慢補也ok。 等需求差不多對齊，Qoder也沒立刻一頭扎進去猛寫程式碼。 它先給了份計劃書，把剛才散落在幾輪對話裡的要求重新捋了一遍。 員工端怎麼做、店長端需要哪些功能、經營頁面展示什麼資料、各個頁面之間怎麼聯動，都被拆成了一項項具體任務。 這時候咱基本就可以撒手了，接下來才是Qoder真正忙活的時候。 建立專案、設計資料結構、生成模擬經營資料、搭頁面、寫互動邏輯，再把營業額、訂單量、客單價這些指標一個個塞進視覺化圖表裡。 沒過多久，一套還真像那麼回事的咖啡店經營系統就跑起來了。 員工端開啟，可以直接檢視自己的班次和工時，還可以提交自己的調班申請； 切到店長端，能看到各個門店的經營總覽，賣了多少單、賺了多少錢一目瞭然； 一週排班情況也鋪在眼前，不同員工在哪家店、上什麼班也非常清楚，剛剛那位員工提交的調班申請也正在等待批准～ 這邊一批准完，員工端那裡也即時更改了狀態。 咱從頭到尾沒寫一行程式碼，一個原本只在嘴上描述的需求，還真變成了能點、能看、能操作的工具！！ 但有一點得說清楚，咱沒Coding，不代表Qoder沒Coding。 把Qoder背後的執行過程翻出來，程式碼是一點沒少寫。 而且 Qoder自己寫的功能還能自己驗貨 。 它可以通過Computer Use和Browser Use進入真實的軟體環境操作，驗證生成的程式碼產物在真實環境下執行是否達標，發現問題後還能回溯修改程式碼，再次完成閉環校驗。 第一把玩下來，確實挺爽。 不過，從0開始做東西，多少還算Coding Agent的舒適區。 這兩年Vibe Coding火成這樣，一句話搓個網頁、小遊戲甚至小應用，大家已經見得不少。 真想看看Qoder的Coding底子夠不夠硬，還是得把它扔進別人寫好的程式碼堆裡。 第二把直接上真專案。 這次咱找來了一個現成的3D太陽系專案。 原專案已經做得相當完整，太陽和八大行星都在，行星沿著各自軌道運動，可以縮放、旋轉視角，還能點選不同星球檢視資訊。 這回不讓Qoder從頭重寫，就在別人已經寫好的專案裡動刀。 需求也給它整點有畫面的： 給太陽系加一個「星際旅行模式」，比如從地球出發前往火星會出現一條星際航線，有一艘小飛船航行。 旁邊增加一個旅行面板，顯示當前進度、飛行狀態和預計抵達時間，鏡頭最好還能跟著飛船一起移動。 這活兒聽起來一句話。真要改，可不是隨便往頁面上塞個按鈕。 Qoder首先得把原來的Repo啃明白，專案用什麼技術棧，太陽和行星怎麼生成，公轉動畫在哪裡控制，場景怎麼渲染，相機又歸誰管…… 別人已經搭好的邏輯不能一腳踹翻，還得找到合適的位置，把新的旅行模式嵌進去。 等專案上下文摸得差不多，Qoder給出修改計劃，才真正開始動刀。 新增旅行模式需要的元件，修改原有場景邏輯，把飛船塞進3D世界，再處理飛行路線、動畫狀態、進度變化和鏡頭控制……改動開始在多個檔案之間鋪開。 改完程式碼之後，Qoder又非常“自覺”地開始自我驗證，進入真實環境實操檢查。 開啟自動審批模式之後，這一整套校驗流程就可以放手交給它，我們只負責最後的結果驗收。 接著咱自己重新啟動專案，試一把星際航行！ 選定兩個星球后，原本只有行星自己轉悠的太陽系裡，多出了一條貝塞爾航線。 點下起航，飛船出發，進度條跟著往前走，鏡頭也開始追著它穿過太陽系。 現實裡的開發工作就是這樣，程式設計師更多時候，接手的是已經跑了幾個月甚至幾年的專案。 所以一個能 讀懂別人的專案，再接著往下開發的工具 才是剛需。 Qoder還支援 40多個聯結器、70多個外掛和2萬多個技能 ，可以將程式碼倉庫、專案管理、雲服務及內部工具等工作系統接入AI工作流。 當然了，Qoder的這些能力並不是桌面端上線後憑空出現的，靠的是過去一年Qoder在Agentic Coding領域沉澱積累下來的技術底子。 首先是上下文理解。 不管是模糊的口頭需求，還是接手一份存量專案倉庫，它都能讀懂專案現狀，抓住使用者背後真正想要達成的目標； 在此基礎上，Goal和Plan負責把目標進一步拆成可執行的路徑； 阿里自研的Agent Harness則把上下文、檔案系統、終端和工具呼叫組織起來，讓一次次模型判斷能夠真正落到Coding執行上，並根據新的執行結果繼續推進。 最後再通過測試，以及Computer Use、Browser Use這樣的環境實操能力進行驗證，發現問題就回到前面的執行環節繼續修改。 前面看起來挺絲滑的「聊著聊著就成了」，拆到底層其實是一條相當完整的執行鏈： 理解→規劃→Coding→執行→驗證→修正 。 整套閉環跑通之後，才得以把底層的Coding能力向外釋放出來。 Coding正在變成AI的數字執行力 大家肯定也很好奇， Qoder明明是個Coding Agent，怎麼幹著幹著，活兒越接越寬了？ 這事兒還得從咱們目前的工作狀態說起。 仔細想想，現在很多人的工作早就有一大半都搬進了數字世界。 網頁、資料、文件、軟體、資料庫、程式碼倉庫、業務系統…… 雖然名字和品類五花八門，但說到底，我們每天都在和這些 數字資產 打交道。 做一個網頁，要修改前端程式碼；處理一批資料，背後可能要跑指令碼；搭一個內部工具，需要建立檔案、實現功能；自動化一套流程，還得呼叫不同的軟體和工具，把原本分散的環節串起來。 這些活兒看起來八竿子打不著，但大家乾的其實都是一件事： 對數字世界裡的資訊和資產進行操作 。 以前的人是怎麼幹這些事的呢？ 最直觀的當然是滑鼠和鍵盤，點按鈕、拖檔案、改表格、複製貼上。 但如果軟體自帶功能不夠用，你想自己搞出新東西，想讓電腦自動批次幹活，這時候就要寫程式碼了。 Coding厲害就厲害在這裡： 可以憑空做出新軟體，一次性處理成千上萬條資料，對接不同系統，把要手動點幾十遍的活直接自動化搞定。 可以說，Coding進一步提供了 創造、改造和連線數字世界的能力 。 這麼一看，Coding Agent的活兒為什麼會越接越寬，也就沒那麼奇怪了。 因為AI Agent今天面對的，其實是同一個問題。 現在大模型會思考、會分析、會規劃方案，但是腦子裡想得出辦法，不等於事情就做完了。 從想好方案，到真正落地做完，中間差了一步 「動手執行」 。 而Coding恰好能補上這一環。 到了Agent時代， Coding不再只是程式設計師開發軟體的專業技能，也正在成為AI進入數字世界之後的一種執行力 。 Coding不只屬於程式設計師了 再回頭看AI Coding這幾年的變化，其實趨勢一直挺清晰： AI越寫越多，人越寫越少。 但當Agent開始接過越來越多實現過程，另一個有意思的變化也隨之出現了： 當越來越多Coding開始由Agent執行，呼叫Coding能力的人，還必須自己會Coding嗎？ Qoder這次做的，就是 讓更多人能用上這種Coding執行能力 。 當然了，這可不意味著以後人人都得轉行當程式設計師。 產品怎麼定義，體驗到底好不好，業務流程該怎麼跑，一個創意值不值得做，這些真正決定結果的判斷，依然來自那些產品經理、設計師、運營。 但專業開發者也不會因此消失。 越是複雜的軟體工程，架構設計、工程質量、關鍵技術判斷和最終審閱，越需要真正的專業能力。 實際上，真正發生變化的，是夾在「想法」和「實現」之間的那一層。 過去一年，Qoder已經在全球600萬用戶和10萬家企業客戶的真實使用裡，打磨好了這套Coding執行能力。 現在，它開始把這套能力交到更多人手裡。 所以，下次腦子裡再突然蹦出個「要不我做個XXX」的念頭—— 先別急著找程式設計師。 把桌寵喊出來嘮兩句，沒準聊著聊著，真就成了。 目前Qoder上線活動已經同步開啟，上線5天內，所有個人使用者每天可以領取500 Credits，是Qwen abstract: OpenClaw：紅過，愛過，散了 夢瑤 2026-08-29 20:00:51 來源： 量子位 龍蝦退潮，Harness上位 夢瑤 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號 QbitAI 這才過去多久啊，咋感覺OpenClaw像沒來過一樣啊。。。（疑惑.jpg） 最近X上網友們對於OpenClaw的集體悼念，真網友看了感慨，龍蝦之父Peter看了流淚。。。 問題是—— 哥們，這玩意兒明明幾個月前還紅得發紫啊！！！ 幾個月前，整個AI圈都在喜迎自己的「賈維斯時刻」。 什麼全民養龍蝦、搶Mac mini、付費上門部署，朋友圈一夜之間人均賽博養殖戶，那個現象級出圈的盛況還歷歷在目。 結果這才過去半年左右的時間，大家已經集體轉頭研究Claude Code、Codex、Skills和Harness了。。。 好好好，AI圈現在連時代的眼淚，保質期都開始按「月」算了。 OpenClaw：所以愛會消失，對嗎？ 從“賈維斯時刻”到時代的眼淚，OpenClaw只用了幾個月 這個世界有時候就這麼魔幻。 很多後來被叫作「時代的眼淚」的東西，剛出現的時候，往往都紅得像是要統治下一個時代。 OpenClaw就是這麼一個典型。（doge） 之所以當時能一下子現象級出圈，主要還是因為這玩意兒，真的太顛覆大家對AI的認知了。。。 那時候大家還在琢磨怎麼把各種AI產品用順手，龍蝦之父Peter直接端出世紀大作OpenClaw—— 一個24小時住在你電腦裡，隨時等你發號施令的AI智慧體。 你可以把它直接裝進Mac、Windows甚至樹莓派裡，再接上Claude、GPT、Gemini、DeepSeek這些模型。 然後把郵箱、瀏覽器、終端、日曆、聊天軟體這些許可權交給它。 接下來，你人甚至都不用守在電腦前。 在Discord、Telegram裡扔過去一句話，它就能自己讀郵件、查資料、寫程式碼、跑指令碼，甚至繼續給自己裝新工具。 這套體驗放到當時，精準命中了所有人對AI Agent最樸素的幻想： 嚯，開源賈維斯真讓人搓出來了！！！ 然後，整個AI圈過年了。 OpenClaw很快從一個開發者專案，火成了一場全民「養蝦運動」。 那段時間，買Mac mini、裝Clawdbot、給自己的Agent起名字，幾乎成了AI圈的新型賽博裝修。 深圳華強北甚至一度出現Mac mini缺貨，部分型號現貨加價最高約600元。 緊接著，大廠也坐不住了。 騰訊百度等大廠搞各種OpenClaw線下安裝活動。 幾十個程式設計師現場支攤，手把手幫幾百個人安裝OpenClaw，網上499上門安裝龍蝦的業務也卷的飛起。 再往後，各家一鍵部署齊刷刷跟進，「養蝦教程」、零門檻版本、各種XX Claw產品滿天飛。 旁觀GitHub，人家Star數也從爬坡改成《旱地拔蔥》模式了。 從2025年11月底上線，到2026年3月3日，差不多100天，OpenClaw直接衝到25萬+Star，順手還把React給超了。 要知道React攢到這個量級，花了十多年，而OpenClaw，只用了三個多月。 到3月底，龍蝦的Star甚至已經進一步衝到33萬+，一度成為GitHub歷史上增長最快的開源專案之一，還有統計顯示，它最高曾在48小時裡狂攬超過3.4萬個Star。 世界就是這麼殘酷，就這麼不給賈維斯留情面。 現在，距離OpenClaw橫空出世也才過去幾個月。 當我重新去社交媒體上搜OpenClaw時，真的已經有點像在考古了。。。 曾經讓全網震驚、眩暈、癱坐的龍蝦，再次被提起時，畫風已經變成了「集體悼念」—— 網友A：OpenClaw本來是要統治世界的，結果現在也沒人再提它了。（笑） 網友B：OpenClaw咋滴了這是，我幾乎看不到有人再提到龍蝦了。。。 網友C更絕：龍蝦徹底涼了吧這是，也沒見有人再討論過這產品了，估計是寄了。 只能說，OpenClaw這波，也算是開局即巔峰，巔峰完就查無此蝦了。。。 龍蝦沒死，但大家已經開始玩“原廠代打”了 說到這兒，先給OpenClaw說句公道話——龍蝦其實沒死！！ 從GitHub資料看，它活得還挺滋潤～ 到了8月，OpenClaw的Star已經一路衝到38萬+，Fork超過8萬；X上相關產品更新也沒停，專案依舊有人開發、有人折騰、有人養蝦。 甚至吧，更準確地說，OpenClaw也不是不火了，而是《春風化雨》了—— 因為「超絕親民版」龍蝦，遊進了各主流廠商的池塘，開始瘋狂繁衍了。。。 今年3月前後，騰訊先後推出WorkBuddy和QClaw，主打一鍵部署，還能直接用微信遠端操控。 百度推出了DuMate+龍蝦全家桶，主打一個桌面蝦、雲端蝦、手機蝦、安全蝦、家用小龍蝦一鍋端。 網易有道也搞出了LobsterAI，支援本地個人Agent、跨平臺執行，以及Skills、MCP、IM遠端控制。 智譜推出的AutoClaw，支援本地一鍵部署OpenClaw，預裝Skills、接入飛書，後面又開始往「自進化」上卷。 火山引擎推出的ArkClaw，也同樣支援7×24小時執行，後續還在往Runtime、多Agent協作擴展。 …… 據不完全統計，單國內廠商推出的龍蝦衍生產品，就有30+款。 換句話說，OpenClaw的名字雖然慢慢淡了，但低門檻、還便宜的蝦苗已經撒滿各家池塘。。。 而這，還只是第一層變化。 因為真正讓屬於OpenClaw自己的「全民養蝦時代」過去的，是AI圈卷的東西已經往下一層走了—— 現如今，Harness當立了。 這其實特別能說明OpenClaw這幾個月經歷了什麼。 大家還記得不，龍蝦最火的時候，最迷人的地方就是：什麼都能自己《攢》。 模型自己挑，許可權自己配，郵箱、瀏覽器、終端自己接，再往裡面一層層塞Skill。 但幾個月過去，Claude Code、Codex這些「原廠選手」已經直接把這一整套體驗給打包端上來了—— OpenAI今年更新Agents SDK時，就明確把檔案操作、命令執行、長任務、沙箱執行這些能力塞進了一套model-native harness；Codex本身也已經形成自己的完整Harness。 怎麼給模型配上下文、記憶、工具、沙箱、許可權、工作流，讓它穩定連續幹活，開始成為了大家當下討論的核心。 只能說，真·一代版本一代神。 當然啦，風口轉向也不能全怪AI圈喜新厭舊。 不知道大家還記不記得，OpenClaw當初最驚豔的那些特點，本身也帶著幾個很現實的「副作用」。 第一個就是：燒錢。 當時「養龍蝦」順手帶火了一波Token焦慮，尤其這種24小時線上的Agent，會不停維護上下文、呼叫模型、呼叫工具、失敗重試，是真燒Token。 於是很多人的養蝦體驗大概是—— 第一天：神了，這不開源賈維斯嘛！？ 第三天：誒？還能這麼玩。 第七天：救啊，我Token呢？ 此外，OpenClaw從出生起，還有另一個一直甩不掉的關鍵詞：安全。 最經典的案例之一，就是Meta安全與協調負責人曾給OpenClaw開放郵箱許可權。 結果好傢伙，龍蝦一頓操作，直接開始刪郵件，而且一度根本停不下來。。。 這件事之所以嚇人，也正好戳中了個人Agent最核心的矛盾——你越想讓它像賈維斯，就越得給它更多許可權；許可權越大，一次失控的代價也越大。 所以吧，我們再回頭看OpenClaw，會發現它其實沒有輸得那麼慘。 感覺龍蝦更像是提前把下一階段Agent真正要解決的問題，全給大家演示了一遍—— 就比如怎麼讓AI擁有手腳，又別讓它亂伸手；怎麼讓它24小時幹活，又別24小時燒錢；怎麼給它足夠自由，又能在出事時把它拽回來。 而今天Claude Code、Codex乃至越來越多Harness在瘋狂補的，恰恰就是這些東西。 所以某種程度上龍蝦留下來的最大遺產，可能已經悄悄從「人人養一個OpenClaw」，變成了： 人人都開始琢磨，怎麼造一個更靠譜的OpenClaw！！ 龍蝦之父現在忙啥呢：跑去給下一代賈維斯蓋廠了 那問題又來了。 龍蝦都快成時代眼淚了，龍蝦之父Peter現在擱哪兒發大財捏？ 答案多少有點節目效果：老哥跑OpenAI造下一代Agent去了。 今年2月，Peter Steinberger正式加入OpenAI，方向也很明確，繼續折騰他最上頭的那件事——個人AI Agent。 加入OpenAI之後，Peter很快就扎進了Codex和Agent相關工作裡。 一邊組團隊，一邊繼續研究怎麼讓Agent更長時間、更穩定地自己幹活。 最近他在採訪和演講裡反覆提到Software Factory這個概念—— 讓一群Agent自己寫程式碼、測試、修Bug、繼續迭代，人主要負責定目標和驗收，甚至他還試過讓Codex圍著一個任務，連續跑上一週。 然後就在這兩天，Peter又出現在了另一個很抽象的新聞裡—— 他和Dropbox聯合創始人Drew Houston一起，各自掏了100萬美元，成為Omacom Foundation的新Founding Patron。 這個基金會幹啥的捏： 認真研究怎麼讓「Linux桌面之年」別再年年跳票。（bushi 說正經的，就是拿錢去養基礎設施、開源專案和開發者，想把Linux桌面真正推向更大規模。 是的，養一隻龍蝦已經滿足不了龍蝦之父了。 這邊OpenClaw都快成賽博文物了。 title: 32GB大視訊記憶體加持，英特爾銳炫Pro B70搞定AI漫劇創作
abstract: 32GB大視訊記憶體加持，英特爾銳炫Pro B70搞定AI漫劇創作 量子位的朋友們 2026-08-29 19:35:57 來源： 量子位 從劇本到成片 今日，英特爾在廣州舉辦以“智算於芯，創想無垠”為主題的AIGC創作研討會。繼日前實現對開源模型MiniMax H3的Day 0首發適配支援後，英特爾在現場聯合MiniMax、數字摺疊展示了基於英特爾銳炫™ Pro B70專業級顯示卡打造的本地化AI影片製作全流程生成方案，並與眾多AI創作者、開發者及影視愛好者，共同探討如何突破算力門檻，高效實現從創意至成品的轉化。 當前，國內AIGC產業迎來爆發式的繁榮發展，影像與影片生成更是增長極為迅猛的核心賽道。但在AI短劇快速崛起的背後，市場不僅對角色一致性、音畫質量及鏡頭的動態連貫性提出了影音級別的高要求，昂貴的算力與複雜的部署更讓大量中小型團隊和個人創作者望而卻步。與此同時，技術能力向少數閉源模型的過度集中，也讓創意表達難以充分施展。
